title: Understanding Ownership
book_sections: 4.1 What Is Ownership? — rules, scope, String, allocation, moves, replacement, Clone/Copy, functions and returns.
4.2 References and Borrowing — shared access, mutable access, last use, dangling references and borrow rules.
4.3 The Slice Type — string slices, literals, flexible parameters and array slices.
Course additions: the foundation’s Unicode-aware text loops and string helper methods.
objectives: Explain the stack-frame and heap model, create owned text, and trace its owner and cleanup.
Trace a String assignment, repair E0382, and explain replacement without inventing a second owner.
Distinguish copied values, copied shared references, moved ownership and independent String clones.
Follow owned values into functions and return ownership to callers, including tuples.
Read a borrowed value without consuming its owner and recognize a shared reference’s restrictions.
Mutate through exclusive access, arrange borrows by last use, and return owned values instead of dangling references.
Borrow text or array windows, choose safe UTF-8 boundaries, and process Unicode text with taught loop APIs.

lessons.title: The stack, the heap and scope
lessons.objective_md: Explain the stack-frame and heap model, create owned text, and trace its owner and cleanup.

screens.heading: Instructions, literals and runtime data
screens.text_md:
Compiling turns Rust code into executable instructions. Literal text such as `"hi"` is data stored as part of the program.

Running `main` also creates values. `String::from(literal)` builds separately owned, mutable text; it does not change the literal.

In this model, **call-local storage** holds `main`’s working values. **Heap storage** is separately allocated space used for the growable `String` buffer. The next screens explain call frames, ownership and cleanup.

This is an explanatory picture, with no promised addresses or physical placement.

coming_from.c: C arrays need explicit bounds and allocation discipline. C++ std::string owns its buffer too; Rust adds compile-time ownership rules.
coming_from.go: Go strings are immutable byte sequences with managed storage. Rust `String` is growable UTF-8 text whose owner releases its buffer.
coming_from.java: Java and C# strings are immutable, with managed memory. Rust `String` can grow and its owner controls cleanup without a tracing garbage collector.
coming_from.js: JavaScript strings are immutable values. Rust `String` is owned growable UTF-8 text; ownership determines who cleans it up.
coming_from.python: Python names can share a mutable list; `String` has one owner. A Python str is immutable, so compare the operations rather than assuming identical storage.

steps.visual_md: Owner panel: literal reads the program text; owned owns separate mutable text; data panel: static hi and separately owned hi

screens.heading: A value has an owner
screens.text_md: An owner is responsible for a value. In our examples, a local binding owns a `String`. There is one owner of that `String` value at a time. When that owner leaves its scope, the value is dropped unless ownership has moved away.

screens.heading: Calls add frames; returns remove them
screens.text_md: A stack frame holds a call’s working state in our model. Calling a function adds its frame above the caller; returning removes the newest frame first: last in, first out. The compiler may keep local values in registers, small storage locations inside the processor. Here the `u32` result is returned to main. Heap buffers have a separate lifetime controlled by ownership, not just by removing a frame.

screens.heading: A memory model, not a placement promise
screens.text_md: Think of the stack as call-local storage and the heap as separately allocated storage. A pointer identifies a memory location. Calling `text.len()` reads the current UTF-8 byte length. A `String` is represented by a pointer, length, and capacity; its UTF-8 buffer is heap allocated when needed. Empty Strings need no buffer allocation. Compiler optimizations and storing values inside other data structures can change physical placement.

screens.heading: Growing and releasing a heap buffer
screens.text_md: `push_str(" there")` appends the supplied text to the `String`; this method needs a mutable owner. The allocator provides storage for owned text. Length is used bytes; capacity is reserved bytes. Appending can reuse spare capacity or grow the allocation, possibly relocating it. We show both permitted outcomes rather than inventing an address or capacity. At scope exit, an unmoved `String` releases its allocation; this does not promise that the operating system immediately reclaims those pages.

screens.text_md: `String::new`() starts empty; `String::from` and a literal’s .to_string() create owned text. A literal such as "hi" has type `&str` and refers to fixed text in the program. Use push for one `char` and push_str for a string. These method calls hide the borrowing details until L4.5–6.

screens.heading: Length counts bytes
screens.text_md: UTF-8 uses different byte lengths for different scalars. len() counts bytes; is_empty() tests whether that count is zero. A `char` is one Unicode scalar value, not necessarily one visible character. We will count and slice text safely in L4.7.

screens.text_md: format! uses the familiar formatting syntax but returns a `String` instead of printing. For these arguments it reads the values without moving their ownership. Assigning its result replaces the old `String` and drops that old value. This convenient rebuilding is acceptable in small early exercises.

Not quite. len only reads the existing String. No ownership transfer or conflicting mutation occurs in this program.

lessons.title: Moves
lessons.objective_md: Trace a `String` assignment, repair E0382, and explain replacement without inventing a second owner.

screens.heading: Follow the ownership arrow
screens.text_md: Assignment transfers ownership of this non-`Copy` value. The text does not need to be duplicated. The old binding becomes unusable; it is not an empty `String`. The animation models the ownership change rather than guaranteeing a machine-level copy. The right-hand side supplies the value; the left-hand side receives it. Here let initializes a new binding.

coming_from.c: C++ std::string ordinary assignment normally copies; move assignment can transfer its storage. A moved-from C++ string remains valid with unspecified contents; Rust rejects reading a moved binding until reinitialized.
coming_from.go: Go slice assignment copies a header and allows aliases. Rust `String` assignment transfers ownership instead; both names cannot keep using the owned `String`.
coming_from.java: Java/C# object variables can share a managed object. Rust `String` assignment leaves one usable owner rather than two aliases with mutable access.
coming_from.js: JavaScript object assignment copies a reference. Rust `String` assignment transfers its ownership; this comparison concerns objects, not immutable JavaScript string semantics.
coming_from.python: Python assignment can bind two names to one mutable object. Assigning a Rust `String` transfers ownership and invalidates the old binding’s value.

screens.heading: Why the old owner is invalid
screens.text_md: If two independent owners each freed the same buffer, cleanup would be unsafe. Rust `String` avoids that by transferring responsibility once. Other languages use their own copying or managed-memory rules; they do not universally crash on assignment.

screens.heading: Reassignment needs a mutable destination
screens.text_md: In `s1 = s2`, s2 supplies the value and s1 receives it. Unlike let initialization, replacing an initialized binding needs mut on the destination. Moving out of s2 does not itself require mut. This rejected example needs let mut s1; adding mut to s2 would not fix the error.

lessons.title: Clone and Copy
lessons.objective_md: Distinguish copied values, copied shared references, moved ownership and independent `String` clones.

screens.heading: Clone creates independent text
screens.text_md: For `String`, clone makes another owned copy of the text. It does not transfer ownership out of the original. A clone costs time and storage proportional to the text; empty strings may need no allocation.

coming_from.c: C++ std::string copies by default; Rust requests that copy with clone. Rust `Copy` is a type capability, not a synonym for stack placement.
coming_from.go: Go scalar assignment copies values, and slice assignment shares backing storage. Rust `Copy` scalars also copy, but `String::clone` creates independent text.
coming_from.java: Java/C# assignment of objects shares references. Rust `String::clone` creates independent text, while integers remain usable after ordinary assignment.
coming_from.js: JavaScript object spread is a shallow copy. Rust `String::clone` duplicates the text; simple `Copy` values are copied automatically on assignment.
coming_from.python: Python copy operations depend on the type and can be shallow. `String::clone` creates independent owned text; changing it does not alter the original.

screens.heading: Integer assignment copies the value
screens.text_md: Integers implement `Copy`. In `s1 = s2`, s1 receives a copy and s2 remains usable. Changing s1 does not change s2. `Copy` is a type capability; it is not a promise that the value physically lives on the stack. Assignment to an already initialized s1 still requires a mutable destination.

screens.text_md: A tuple or array is `Copy` when all its elements are `Copy`. Copying an array copies its elements; a large `Copy` value may still take substantial work. We do not define or derive custom `Copy` types in this chapter.

screens.heading: String moves; Copy is not about allocation
screens.text_md: `String` does not implement `Copy`. Even an empty `String::new()` with no allocated buffer moves on assignment. Assignment transfers its owned value and leaves the source unusable, regardless of where the `String` descriptor physically resides. Custom types without `Copy` also move, even with only numeric fields. Chapter 5 will compare custom structs with and without `Copy`; a struct owning a `String` cannot implement `Copy`.

lessons.title: Ownership and functions
lessons.objective_md: Follow owned values into functions and return ownership to callers, including tuples.

screens.heading: An owned argument moves into the call
screens.text_md: An owned `String` argument moves into the callee’s parameter. The caller frame waits while the callee frame is active. If the callee does not return the `String`, its parameter drops at the end of that call and releases the buffer. Popping a frame and freeing a heap buffer are different events; ownership decides whether the buffer survives.

coming_from.c: C++ value parameters may copy or move based on the call. Rust `String` value arguments move unless explicitly cloned.
coming_from.go: Go copies argument values, with slice headers still sharing data. Rust `String` value arguments transfer their ownership.
coming_from.java: Java/C# object arguments copy references. Passing Rust `String` by value transfers ownership to the called function.
coming_from.js: JavaScript object parameters share access to the object. Rust function signatures distinguish ownership transfer from borrowing.
coming_from.python: Python function parameters can reference an existing object. A Rust `String` parameter takes ownership unless its type is a reference.

screens.heading: Return ownership to the caller
screens.text_md: Returning a `String` transfers ownership to the caller before the callee frame ends. Its buffer remains live because the caller receives the owned value. Frame removal therefore does not mean freeing every allocation used during that call. Appending may grow or relocate the buffer; returning ownership does not itself require cloning.
